title: The Yin And Yang Of Classroom Management
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin diagnoses a common failure mode among teachers working to improve classroom management: they tighten up so much on consistency and accountability that they suppress their own personality, becoming tense and 'no fun,' which improves short-term behavior but damages the relationship and joy that make a classroom genuinely work. His central metaphor is a yin-yang balance between two forces that must be pursued simultaneously rather than traded off against each other: rigorous, every-single-time accountability defined by a classroom management plan, and an authentic embrace of humor, openness, and warmth that builds rapport and charisma. He argues that in the current educational climate, likability is no longer optional -- real impact requires both extremes pushed as far as possible, not a moderate middle ground, describing it as extending 'the yin-yang envelope' until behavior changes. He grounds the claim autobiographically, describing 15 years of testing and refining this two-pronged approach since starting his own career with non-negotiable accountability paired with more playfulness than he'd recommend to others today.
points: Tightening classroom management often causes teachers to suppress their own personality, improving short-term behavior at the cost of relationship and classroom joy.
The two forces -- strict, consistent accountability and authentic warmth/humor -- must be pursued as extremes simultaneously, not balanced toward a moderate middle.
Likability is framed as no longer optional but required for real behavioral and academic impact in the current era.
The approach was built over roughly 15 years of personal testing and adjustment, starting from a rougher combination of non-negotiable accountability and heavy playfulness.
quotes: A danger in trying to improve classroom management is that you tighten up.

But the result is that while behavior improves in the short term, your classroom becomes less desirable. Your relationship with your class suffers. The joy of learning and coming to school deteriorates.

It’s the extremes of every-single-time accountability—defined by your classroom management plan—combined with the authentic embrace of your personality that creates a well-behaved classroom that students love.
Only by tightening your consistency and loosening your “self” can you create the leverage to move your students in the direction you want them to go.
In this day and age, one without the other will fail. Real impact, the kind that results in galloping academic motivation and achievement, must contain sky-high standards and a teacher students like.
I spent the next 15 years or so testing, adjusting, and reverse-engineering everything I was doing day-to-day to create the exact individual strategies that support this secret.
